## Pollinator dataset {#sec-dataset_pollinators .core}

[**Core**]{.core-text}

We will use this research dataset repeatedly throughout both this practical and Practical 6 (Further Statistics) and visit others as needed.

The main dataset we will use in this practical is [pan-trap survey data](https://catalogue.ceh.ac.uk/documents/9df83130-e98f-48b0-bbfc-32f5920eedb0) from the UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme (PoMS). In this scheme, multiple [pan-traps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_trap) are set in each of a set of specific 1km squares across the UK. On four days each summer, volunteers will set out traps for six hours, then send the insects to be counted. Flowering plants within a 2m radius of the trap are also recorded.

[comment]: todo_katy link to the preprocessing.

The data from the scheme is provided as data per trap, for this practical we have amalgamated the data across all dates and across each 1km square. 

You have been provided with three data files:

* In the **insect counts** CSV file - `data/insect_counts.csv` each row represents a combination of an insect species and a sampling site, and the total number of times that insect was observed at that site. Many of the counts will be zero.

* In the **flower counts** CSV file - `data/flower_counts.csv` each row represents a combination of a flower species and a sampling site, plus TRUE or FALSE depending if that flower was ever observed within 2m of the site.

* In the **site metadata** CSV file - `data/site_metadata.csv`, each row represents a single 1km square sampling site. The data frame contains information about the geographical location, plus land use and climate at the sample site. Additional climate data has been added based on [WorldClim](https://nordata.physics.utoronto.ca/en/annexes-datasets-descriptions/72-precipitation/worldclim-version-2/) data, which has detailed climate data by square averaged from 1970-2000. Various additional statistics have been calculated based on the information in the original data frame.

<details>
<summary>Data citation</summary>

The UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme (PoMS) is a partnership funded jointly by UKCEH and JNCC (through funding from Defra, Scottish Government, Welsh Government, and DAERA). UKCEH’s contribution is funded by the Natural Environment Research Council award number NE/R016429/1 as part of the UK-SCAPE programme delivering National Capability. Between 2017 and 2021, PoMS was funded by UKCEH and Defra (England), Welsh Government, Scottish Government, DAERA (Northern Ireland), and JNCC.
PoMS is indebted to the many volunteers who carry out surveys and contribute data to the scheme.

</details>

::: {.callout-exercise #ex_summarise_bees .rec}

### Revise data frame operations

[**Recommended**]{.rec-text}

If you haven't already, create a new Quarto file, `pollinators.qmd`.

::: {.callout-note .copycode #copy-poll}

### Include this code

```{r start_poll, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
set.seed(42)
```

:::

In your `pollinators.qmd` Quarto file:

* Read the three CSV files:

  * `data/insect_counts.csv`
  * `data/flower_counts.csv`
  * `data/site_metadata.csv`

* Count how many unique sites there are. Site ID is in the `x1km_square` column of the insect counts data frame and site metadata data frame. 
* Count how many observations of insects there are - including multiple observations of the same insect at the same site. Number of observations is in the `n_observed` column of the insect counts data frame.
* Find the insect species which was observed most frequently and how many times it was observed. Insect species is in the column `species` of the insect counts data frame.

::: {.callout-note #note-arrange}

The `arrange()` function sorts the rows of a data frame based on the values in a column. By default, values are arranged from smallest to largest, or from A to Z.

```{r arrange_intro}
ppg <- tibble(
  name = c("Blossom", "Buttercup", "Bubbles"),
  height = c(60, 62, 58)
)

gt(ppg)
```

```{r arrange_by_height}
by_height <- ppg |>
  arrange(height)
gt(by_height)
```

To arrange the values from largest to smallest, or Z to A, we can use the `desc()` function inside `arrange()`.

```{r arrange_by_height_rev}
by_height_r <- ppg |>
  arrange(desc(height))
gt(by_height_r)
```

:::

::: {.callout-answer #ex_summarise_bees_ans}

[Read the three CSV files]{.blue-text}

```{r summarise_bees_ans1, message=FALSE}
insect_counts <- read_csv("data/insect_counts.csv")
flower_counts <- read_csv("data/flower_counts.csv")
site_metadata <- read_csv("data/site_metadata.csv")
```

[Count how many unique sites there are. Site ID is in the `x1km_square` column of the insect counts data frame and site metadata data frame. ]{.blue-text}

```{r summarise_bees_ans2, message=FALSE}
site_count <- nrow(site_metadata)
print(site_count)
```
There are `r site_count` sites.

[Count how many observations of insects there are - including multiple observations of the same insect at the same site. Number of observations is in the `n_observed` column of the insect counts data frame]{.blue-text}

```{r summarise_bees_ans3, message=FALSE}
total_insect_obs <- insect_counts |>
  pull(n_observed) |>
  sum()
print(total_insect_obs)
```
There are `r format(total_insect_obs, scientific=FALSE)` insect observations.

[Find the insect species which was observed most frequently and how many times it was observed. Insect species is in the column `species` of the insect counts data frame.]{.blue-text}

```{r summarise_bees_ans4, message=FALSE}
insect_totals <- insect_counts |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(n_obs = sum(n_observed))

insect_totals <- insect_totals |>
  arrange(desc(n_obs))

gt(head(insect_totals))
```

The most commonly observed species was `r pull(insect_totals, species)[1]`, which was observed `r pull(insect_totals, n_obs)[1]` times.

:::
:::


## Examining data {#sec-examining_data .core}

[**Core**]{.core-text}

For now, let's concentrate on a single species, the "bronze furrow bee" *Halictus tumulorum*. This is a relatively common bee species in the UK. It is a species of sweat bee, named because they are often attracted to sweat (although the UK ones usually aren't). 

![*Halictus tumulorum* [Source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halictus_tumulorum#/media/File:Halictus_tumulorum_female,_Bagillt,_North_Wales,_July_2016_3_-_Flickr_-_janetgraham84.jpg)](images/bee.jpg){#fig-bee width="50%" fig-alt="A photo of H. tumulorum"}

We can built hypotheses about the relationship between different variables and the presence or absence of *H. tumulorum* at each site. To do this, we need a data frame with a column which shows if *H. tumulorum* is present or absent at each site.

We can create an extra column in a data frame using the function `mutate()`. 

For example, if I wanted to create a column named `Is_England` in the `site_metadata` data frame showing if a site was in England or not, I could do the following:

```{r mutate}
site_metadata_exp <- site_metadata |>
  mutate(Is_England = country == "England")
gt(head(site_metadata_exp))
```

Here, `country == "England"` is evaluated for each row, so `Is_England` contains `TRUE` for sites in England and `FALSE` for other sites.

We can use any kind of **comparison operator** with mutate (see @sec-comparisons). 

We can also add an existing vector as a new column, or set every row of a new column to the same value.

```{r mutate_3}
# Fixed value
site_metadata_exp <- site_metadata_exp |>
  mutate(new_col_2 = "hello")

gt(head(site_metadata_exp))
```


::: {.callout-exercise #ex-filter_ht .core}

### Build *H. tumulorum* data frame.

[**Core**]{.core-text}

If you haven't already, create a new Quarto file, `pollinators.qmd`.

::: {.callout-note .copycode #copy-poll}

### Include this code

```{r start_poll2, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
set.seed(42)
```

:::


In your `pollinators.qmd` Quarto document:

* Filter the `insect_counts` data frame to include only the counts for *H. tumulorum*.
* Create a logical (see @sec-variable_types) column showing if *H. tumulorum* is detected or undetected at each site using `mutate()` based on the `n_observed` column - if `n_observed` is > 0, this species was detected.
* Join the resulting data frame with the `site_metadata` data frame using `inner_join()`, to add additional site data.
* Store the resulting data frame as a variable named `ht_df`.
* Write the data frame to the file `output/ht_df.csv`.

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true" #ex_filter_ht_ans}
[Filter the `insect_counts` data frame to include only the counts for *H. tumulorum*.]{.blue-text}

```{r subset_ht}
ht_counts <- insect_counts |>
  filter(species == "Halictus tumulorum")
gt(head(ht_counts))
```

[Create a logical (see @sec-variable_types) column showing if *H. tumulorum* is detected or undetected at each site using `mutate()` based on the `n_observed` column - if `n_observed` is > 0, this species was detected.]{.blue-text}

```{r logical_ht}
ht_df <- ht_counts |>
  mutate(detected = n_observed > 0)
```

[Join the resulting data frame with the `site_metadata` data frame using `inner_join()`, to add additional site data.]{.blue-text}

[Store the resulting data frame in as a variable named `ht_df`.]{.blue-text}

```{r presence_absence_ht, message=FALSE}
ht_df <- ht_df |>
  inner_join(site_metadata)

gt(head(ht_df))
```

[Write the data frame to the file `output/ht_df.csv`.]{.blue-text}

```{r save_ht}
write_csv(ht_df, "output/ht_df.csv")
```

:::
:::

*H. tumulorum* tend to be found [towards the south](https://bwars.com/bee/halictidae/halictus-tumulorum) of the UK. Let's use our data to explore the possibility that this is because they don't like very cold temperatures.

We have a column in our site metadata data frame which can help us establish if this is true - the `min_temp_coldest_month` column. This is a BIOCLIM climate variable describing the lowest temperature in the coldest month in the map square and is the mean from 1970-2000. Technically, the lowest tempeature in the coldest month might not be the overall lowest temperature, however, for brevity from here forward we will refer to this just as **minimum temperature**.

We can compare this minimum temperature for the sites where the bees are present and absent using a box plot.

For clarity, let's select only the relevant columns in our data frame, using the `select()` function.

::: {.callout-note .copycode #copy-select}

### Include this code

In `pollinators.qmd`:

```{r select_ht}
ht_temp_df <- ht_df |>
  select(x1km_square, detected, min_temp_coldest_month)
```

:::

```{r show_ht}
gt(head(ht_temp_df))
```

For convenience later, we can calculate the mean, standard deviation and number of observations for sites with and without *H. tumulorum*, using the `group_by()` and `summarise()` functions we learned in @sec-summary_stats.

To do this, use the following code, which you should include in your `pollinators.qmd` Quarto document.

::: {.callout-note .copycode #copy-select}

### Include this code

```{r summary_ht}
ht_temp_summ <- ht_temp_df |>
  group_by(detected) |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(min_temp_coldest_month),
    sd = sd(min_temp_coldest_month),
    count = n()
  )

# Separate present and absent sites
present <- ht_temp_summ |>
  filter(detected == TRUE)

absent <- ht_temp_summ |>
  filter(detected == FALSE)

gt(ht_temp_summ)
```

Present only

```{r show_pres}
gt(present)
```

Absent only

```{r show_abs}
gt(absent)
```

:::


:::{.callout-exercise #ex-boxplot_bees .rec}

### Box plot

[**Recommended**]{.rec-text}

In your `pollinators.qmd` Quarto document, plot a box plot showing the value of `min_temp_coldest_month` in your `ht_df` data frame for the regions with and without these bees (i.e. based on the `detected` column).

* The R function `geom_boxplot()` draws a box plot.
* The `aes` function for this type of plot requires a categorical x variable and a continuous y variable as arguments - so you would use the arguments `x = detected` and `y = min_temp_coldest_month`. 

:::{.callout-answer collapse="true" #ex-boxplot_bees_ans}

```{r boxplot_ht}
#| fig-alt: "Box plot comparing minimum temperature at sites where H. tumulorum was detected and not detected. The detected group is shifted towards higher temperatures, although the two distributions overlap. The undetected box has a longer interquartile range and longer whiskers"
ggplot(
  ht_df,
  aes(x = detected, y = min_temp_coldest_month, fill = detected)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  ggtitle("Minimum Temperature with and without H. tumulorum - Observed") +
  xlab("Presence of H. tumulorum") +
  ylab("Minimum temperature (°C)") +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::
:::
Looking at our box plot, it seems like perhaps these bees don't like the cold.

### Summary

#### Concepts

- Data frames can be **sorted** according to the values in a column, in either ascending or descending order, using `arrange()` and `desc()`. ([Recommended]{.rec-text})

#### Functions

| Function | What it does | Level |
|---|---|---|
| `arrange()` | Sorts the rows of a data frame according to the values in one or more columns. | Recommended |
| `desc()` | Reverses the sorting order within `arrange()`, for example from largest to smallest. | Recommended |
| `nrow()` | Returns the number of rows in a data frame. | Recommended |
